Those who just now had snatched the Christians to punishments, soon sending word to their own error, underwent the same punishments with a joyful mind amid any sorrows. Shame remained for the enemies of the truth, while the greatest praise and glory remained for the Martyrs. Even today, not only Spain but the whole Christian world, as far as it lies open, execrates the former and admires the virtue of the latter, and honors them with deserved praises. Among them are those whom Spain affects with greater honors than they themselves would want if they were alive, for it pursues those, because of their zeal for religion, with religious worship. If they were to return to life, they would undoubtedly complain more about the excessive honors than about the most bitter pains they once suffered. Truly, it is neither wondrous to say nor difficult to believe that, among so many examples of true piety, there existed in Spain those who stained the sincerity of religion with new opinions. No century is fruitful in virtues that is altogether sterile of vices, nor does the wheat easily lack mixed tares. What wonder that these also were born in Spain? Especially the heresy of the <term>GNOSTICS</term> <gloss>those having secret knowledge</gloss> excited great disturbances there. It had its origin in Egypt. Soon its ruin also involved Spain. §. 19.
De formatione membranae testae.

Membrana testae ad albuminis superficiem externam in ultimo primum tractu oviductus, qui inter ejus isthmum et uterum versatur, accedit. Prima intrat pars ovi acutior, membranamque induit, ita ut in obtusiori albumen saepe nudum adhuc visendum sit. Sub hoc nisu tractus isthmicus adeo expanditur, ut plicae membranae interioris penitus deleantur atque maxima tensio habeatur strictioris plane partis oviductus, ubi fors major irritatio membranae succum densiorem quo membrana paretur, elicit. Notanda porro interruptio brevis plicarum muciferarum plane sub isthmi strictura, quo intervallum inter secretionem albuminosam et membranaceam efficitur et fors conditio sistitur formandi ligamenti albuminosi in parte ovi acutiori. Membrana testae duplex paratur, interior fibris microscopicis rectis contexta est, exterior texturam peculiarem non offert *. (*Fig. XXV.*)

The muscular fibers of the mesometrium especially accomplish this movement, as they bend, twist, and constrict the oviduct by drawing it this way and that. The part of its mucous membrane that surrounds the yolk then secretes albumen in the form of membranes, which continuously adheres to this yolk. But the part before and behind the yolk, contracted upon itself, allows the secreted albumen only the form of a cord, which, driven forward in a spiral, twists upon itself and accumulates at either pole of the egg; generally, by this torsion, it returns to the root where it attaches to the yolk, and disappears there into the remaining albumen. (*Fig. XXIV.*) The fact that the chalazae are attached at the side of the axis of the yolk seems to serve the purpose of always pulling the center of gravity of the yolk toward their side, whereby the <term>cicatricula</term> <gloss>germinal disc</gloss> always occupies the uppermost position on the yolk, situated nearest to receive the warmth of the brooding hen.

When you spin the egg very rapidly with a mechanical apparatus, the chalazae do not acquire more numerous twists from this motion, but the untwisted ligament of albumen is torn away from the shell.

§. 19.
*On the formation of the shell membrane.*

The shell membrane first attaches to the outer surface of the albumen in the final tract of the oviduct, which lies between its isthmus and the uterus. The narrower end of the egg enters first and puts on the membrane, so that on the blunter end the albumen is often still to be seen bare. Under this exertion, the isthmic tract expands so greatly that the folds of the inner membrane are completely smoothed away, and the greatest tension occurs in this plainly narrower part of the oviduct, where perhaps a greater irritation of the membrane draws forth a thicker fluid from which the membrane is prepared. Furthermore, one should note the brief interruption of the mucous folds directly below the constriction of the isthmus, by which a pause between the secretion of the albumen and that of the membrane is produced, and perhaps the condition is provided for forming the ligament of albumen at the narrower end of the egg. A double shell membrane is prepared: the inner layer is woven of straight microscopic fibers, while the outer layer presents no distinctive structure *. (*Fig. XXV.*)

---

* In the egg of the grass snake <note>original: "Colubri Natricis"</note>, this inner layer consists of most beautiful wavy fibers; compare G. R. and L. Ch. Treviranus, *Vermischte Schriften*, vol. 1, page 142.

Even if such a disorder could have been prevented with guards of armed men, it was still a certain thing that the public death of such principal subjects, so tenderly loved by the people of his state, would have caused such pity and such an alteration of minds in his <term>Vaſſalli</term> <gloss>Vassals</gloss> that they would have left nothing undone to avenge it over time. 

All these considerations had made him flee from the ordinary remedy of purging the body of his state of those malignant humors with which he saw it filled. He avoided those canonical medicines which, through the abundance of even more pernicious humors they would have stirred up, would have notably worsened the disease. He argued it was a trivial <term>precetto politico</term> <gloss>political precept</gloss> that in the squares and other public places, one should frighten the vile rabble from committing crimes only with the spectacle of <note>original: "ſoggetti meccanici"; meaning low-born or manual laborers</note> common criminals. 

However, for qualified persons loved by the people, whose lives Princes took only for the peace of their states, it was necessary that death and burial be joined with their capture in very secret places. This is because the display of punishments for very distinguished men on high <term>catafalchi</term> <gloss>scaffolds or platforms</gloss> did not generate fear, but a great rage for revenge in everyone. Apollo then asked the Prince how long he had known this precept he had mentioned.

translation: provided for us everything that is good in life; and there is a time when I must be bold before you. <margin>Because he is someone who loves to learn</margin> Being someone who loves to learn, and having been very diligent with discourses concerning wisdom, at first I seemed to him to be very wise, and to many other philosophers; and finally even to myself. And then I tried to demonstrate to him that he believed he was wise, but was not. From there, I became hateful to this man and to many of those present; but as I went away, I reasoned with myself and thought that I was wiser than he. For even though this man thinks he knows something when he does not, just as I do not know, I also do not think [that I know]. I seem, therefore, to be wiser than he by this small thing: that I do not think I know what I do not know. From there, I went to another of those who seemed to be wiser than he, and the same thing appeared to me, and there I became hateful to him and to many others as well. After this, therefore, I went in order, perceiving and grieving and fearing that I was becoming hated, yet it seemed necessary to consider the matter of the god as of the highest importance. Therefore, I had to go to everyone who seemed to know something, while examining what the oracle says. And by the Dog <note>a typical Socratic oath, "by the Dog" refers to the Egyptian god Anubis or is simply a substitute for a stronger oath</note>, men of Athens, for I must tell you the truth, I suffered something like this: those who were most highly esteemed seemed to me to be almost the most deficient when I was searching according to the god, while others who seemed more common were better men regarding being sensible. I must, therefore, show you my wandering as one laboring through certain trials, so that the prophecy might be rendered irrefutable for me. For after the politicians, I went to the poets, those of the tragedies and those of the dithyrambs and the others, as if I would there catch myself being more ignorant than they. Taking up their poems, which seemed to me to be the most elaborately crafted by them, I would ask them what they meant, so that I might also learn something from them. I am ashamed, therefore, to tell you the truth, men, yet it must be spoken. For to put it simply, almost everyone present could speak better than they did about what they themselves had composed. I realized, therefore, also concerning the poets in a short time, that they do not create what they create by wisdom, but by a certain nature and while inspired, just like the divine seers and oracle-speakers. For these, too, say many and beautiful things, but know nothing of what they say. The poets appeared to me to have suffered some such experience, and at the same time I perceived that they, because of their poetry, believed themselves to be the wisest of men in other things, which they were not. I went away, therefore, even from there believing that I had an advantage for the same reason that I had over the politicians. Finally, then, I went to the craftsmen; for I was conscious of myself knowing nothing, so to speak, and I knew that I would find them knowing many and beautiful things. And I was not mistaken in this, but they knew things that I did not know, and they were wiser than I. But, men of Athens, they seemed to me to have the same fault as the poets and the good craftsmen: because they worked their craft well, each claimed to be wisest in other greatest things, and this very mistake of theirs concealed that wisdom. So that I asked myself on behalf of the oracle whether I would prefer to be as I am, neither wise in their wisdom nor ignorant in their ignorance, or to have both things that they have. I answered, therefore, to myself and to the oracle that it was profitable for me to be as I am. From this very examination, men of Athens, many hatreds have arisen for me, and such as are most difficult and burdensome, so that many slanders have arisen from them, and this name is spoken: to be wise. For those present each time think that I myself am wise in those things in which I refute another. But it is likely, men, that the god is truly wise, and that in this oracle he is saying this: that human wisdom is worth little or nothing. And he appears to be speaking of this Socrates, and to have used my name, making me an example, as if he were to say that this one of you, O men, is wisest, who, like Socrates, has recognized that he is worth nothing in truth regarding wisdom. These things, therefore, I still even now go about seeking and investigating according to the god, if I think anyone of the citizens or foreigners is wise. And whenever it does not seem so to me, I help the god by demonstrating that he is not wise. And because of this occupation, I have had no leisure to do anything worth mentioning for the city nor for my own affairs, but I am in ten thousand poverties because of my service to the god. In addition to these things, the young men who follow me, to whom there is most leisure, the sons of the wealthiest, do this of their own accord; they enjoy hearing men being examined, and they themselves often imitate me, and then attempt to examine others. And then, I think, they find an abundance of men who think they know something, but know little or nothing. From there, those who are examined by them become angry with me, not with themselves, and say that there is a certain Socrates who is most abominable and corrupts the youth. And whenever someone asks them what he does and what he teaches, they have nothing to say but are ignorant, but so that they do not seem to be at a loss, they say these ready-made things against all who philosophize: that he investigates the things in the heavens and under the earth, and does not believe in gods, and makes the weaker argument the stronger. For the truth, I think, they would not be willing to speak, that they become exposed as pretending to know, while knowing nothing. As, therefore, I think, they are ambitious and vehement and many, and speaking in an organized and persuasive manner about me, they have filled your ears, slandering me both long ago and vehemently. From these, Meletus set upon me, and Anytus and Lycon; Meletus, being distressed on behalf of the poets; Anytus, on behalf of the craftsmen and the politicians; and Lycon, on behalf of the rhetoricians. So that, as I was saying at the beginning, I would be surprised if I were able to remove this slander from you in such a short time, having become so great. These are the truths for you, men of Athens, and I say them to you without hiding or holding back anything great or small. And yet I know that I am hated for these same things, which is also proof that I speak the truth and that this is my slander and these are its causes. And whether you investigate this now or later, you will find it so. Concerning, then, what my first accusers were accusing me of, let this be a sufficient defense.

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>, O Tat, God imparted to each individual man, but Mind <note>original: *mentem*. In the Hermetic tradition, *mens* (Greek: *nous*) represents divine intellect or higher spiritual awareness, distinguished from mere discursive speech or reason (*sermo* / *logos*).</note> He did not impart in this way. Not that He begrudged it, for He begrudges no one, since malice does not come from Him, but rather arises from that which dwells with the souls of men lacking mind. **TAT.** Why, O father, did God not share Mind with all? **TR.** Because He willed, O son, to set it in the midst as a contest and prize for souls. **TAT.** Where did He place it? **TR.** Having filled a wide mixing bowl <note>original: *craterem*. Referring to the celestial krater or vessel in which souls are dipped to be imbued with divine consciousness.</note> with it, He sent a herald, commanding him to announce such things to the souls of men: "Let whichever soul can, plunge herself into this bowl, namely that soul which believes that she will return to Him who sent her down, and knows the purpose for which she was born." Whoever therefore listened to the herald and immersed themselves in Mind became partakers of knowledge, and receiving Mind, turned out to be perfect men. But those who neglected the proclamation, though partakers of speech, remained devoid of Mind, left in ignorance both of the purpose for which and by whom they were begotten. Moreover, the senses of these men resemble the senses of an irrational beast; thus, entangled in desire, they by no means admire those things worthy of contemplation, for being enslaved to the lusts of the body, they believe that man was born for the sake of these.

<summary>Hermes explains to Tat that while all humans possess speech, God offered divine Mind as a prize in a great mixing bowl, which only those souls who consciously immerse themselves can obtain to achieve spiritual perfection and true knowledge.</summary>

# Hertochdom Milanen.

Dit Hertochdom wordt voor het befte Hertochdom der geheelder Chriftenheyt gheacht, ghelijck Vlaenderen het befte Graeffchap; ghelijck wij te dyer plaetfen ghefeyt hebben. Het is een feer coftelyck ende vruchtbaer landt (gelijck om fegghen geheel Lombardyen is, daert een deel af is), de principael ftadt daer in is Milanen, daer 't hertochdom finen naem na heeft. Defe ftadt is feer vermaert ende beker-it geworden deur de oorlogen in onfen tijden, dier tuffchen den Keyfer Carolus de vijfde, en Francifcus de eerfte van dyen naeme Coninck van Vranckrijck om gevoert fijn geweeft; ende oock deur haer Cafteel datter aen leet, dwelck onder alle fterckten der Chriftenheyt eenē grootē naem heeft. Men telt defe ftadt voor eene vande grootfte fteden van Europa: ende fal oock wel metter tijt de ftercfte beeten, waren de mueren ende bolwercken rontsomme volmaect, daer wij An. 1559. aen fagen wercken. Hoewel dat defe ftadt foo groot is ende naer advenant vol volcks, foo is te verwonderen datter de lijfneeringe foo goeden coop is; maer dat maeckt het vruchtbaer aertrijck daerfe in ghelegen is, ende foo veel wateren ende beken daerfe rontsom van wt het gheberchte en de groote Riviere Po mede gedient wordt; waer deur alle dingen die den menfche nootelyck fijn, oft tot vermaeck ende luft begheert worden, overvloedelyck ende goeden coop, ghebracht worden. Soo groote menichte van alderleye Cunften en hantwercken fijn hier, dattet nauwelyck te gelooven en is; alfoo dat in Italien een fpreecwoort is, Wie Italien beteren wilde, moefte Milanen verderven; te weten, dat hun alfoo de Cunftenaren ende wercklieden hier wt verjaecht fijnde, deur geheel Italien ftroyen ende verbreyden fouden. Seer veel coftelycke ende treffelycke edificien ende ghebouwen fijnder, onder de welcke de principaelste is de opperfte Kercke den Dom gheheeten, waer aen de Cunfte met de Coftelyckheyt fchijnen om prijs te vechten. Ick hebbe fomtijts ghefeyt dattet my dochte een Bagge te fyne, om datfe van onder tot boven met Marmoren beelden, ende alderley ander cieraet ende gefnedenwerck foo overvloedelyck van buyten becleet is, datfe fchijnt niet van Steenbouders, maer van Siluerfmeden gemaect te fyne. De andere Kercken ende Heeren-huyfen fouden hier te lanck fijn te befchryven. Maer die een Burgers oft priuaet perfoons huys wil fien, die gae te Milanen ende vraghe nae het huys dat Tomas de Marini Genewois daer heeft laten maken, (ick dencke dattet nu voldaen is) ende dat van buyten en van binnen wel deur fien hebbende, mach hy hem wel voor laten ftaen, algaet hy verde dat hi nerghens gheen coftelycker oft mogelyck diefghelycx fien en fal. Dit meyne ick dat met my fegghen fullen, alle die haer fulcx verftaende, landen ende Steden befocht hebben. Andere fteden onder dit Hertochdom gheleghen, fijn Pauia feer vermaert deur de hooghe fchole dyer is, ende den flach die fynen onfterffelycken naem van haer heeft, ende by haer ghefchiede An. 1525. daer in Francifcus de Coninck van Vranckrijck ghevangen werdt; daer nae Crema, Lodi certijts Laus Pompeia gheheeten, Como van ghelegentheyt feer playfant, ghelijck wij op haer plaetfe fegghen fullen, ende andere.

# Duchy of Milan.

This Duchy is considered the best Duchy of all Christendom, just as Flanders is the best County; as we have said in those places. It is a very precious and fertile land (as is indeed the whole of Lombardy, of which it is a part); the principal city therein is Milan, from which the Duchy has its name. This city is very famous and has become well-known through the wars in our times, which were waged between the Emperor Charles the Fifth and Francis the First of that name, King of France; and also through its Castle that lies there, which has a great name among all the fortresses of Christendom. One counts this city as one of the largest cities of Europe: and it will also likely in time be the strongest, were the walls and bastions round about completed, on which we saw work being done in the year 1559. Although this city is so large and proportionally full of people, it is still to be wondered at that food is so cheap there; but that is caused by the fertile soil in which it is situated, and so many waters and streams with which it is surrounded and served from the mountains and the great river Po; through which all things that are necessary for man, or desired for pleasure and delight, are brought in abundantly and at a good price. So great a multitude of all kinds of arts and crafts are here, that it is hardly to be believed; so that there is a proverb in Italy: "He who would improve Italy, must destroy Milan"; meaning that the artists and workmen, being chased out of here, would scatter and spread through all of Italy. There are very many precious and excellent edifices and buildings, among which the most principal is the supreme church, called the <term>Dom</term> <gloss>Cathedral</gloss>, where art and costliness seem to fight for the prize. A YOUNG hunter found a circular path one day in a prairie, without any trail leading to, or from it. It was smooth and well-beaten, and looked as if footsteps had trod in it recently. ->If a planet that is set <term>combust by the sun</term>, in debilitation, in an enemy’s sign, or retrograde is weak and forms a **Mutthashila**, it is unable to carry the matter forward. Because its light is at its end or in its "face" <note>original: *mukha*; referring to its current degree-position</note>, it does not accomplish the task. ॥ 62 ॥<-

<margin>Or because of the lack of logic, it destroys the result of the Kamboola yoga. ॥ 61 ॥</margin> A **Mutthashila** yoga between the Lord of the Ascendant <note>representing the querent</note> and the Lord of the Matter <note>representing the object of the question</note> is indeed expected. In that context, according to the previously mentioned characteristics, the Moon is a "Void-Traveler" on a void path. Such a Moon does not possess a **Mutthashila** yoga with either the Lord of the Ascendant or the Lord of the Matter. Alternatively, if such a Moon does not even have a connection <note>original: *vayu* or *yuti*</note> with those two, the yoga is known as **Khallasara**. This is not auspicious. In what way? It "destroys the result of the Kamboola." When there is a **Mutthashila** or just a simple yoga, the **Kamboola** is fulfilled. But here, due to the lack of a **Mutthashila** with anyone, it destroys the result. ॥ 61 ॥

Now the characteristics of the **Radyoga** are explained. "Set" etc.: If a planet is set <term>invisible due to the Sun's proximity</term>, or in its sign of debilitation, or in the house of its enemy, or is retrograde, or has "diminished light"—meaning it is devoid of brilliance—such a planet is considered "weak." If a weak planet forms a **Mutthashila** with any lord of a house, that planet, whether at the "face" <note>beginning of a sign</note> or the end, is not a fulfiller of that house's task...

# Imperial Collection of Four Treasuries, Volume 5
The numbers of the combined calculation, which correspond to the changes of the ten thousand things, all originate from the foundation of four. Because one diligently guards these four, one obtains the numbers of the four initial Heaven and Earth states through the symbols of the four energies and the four centers, thus residing in the correct middle position of the four directions. In this way, one can summarize the origins of all things and encompass the fundamentals of the numbers. All other numbers in the <term>Yi</term> change according to events and do not maintain a constant measure, but the four of the four-fold path is never altered. This is the reason why.

Four emerges from two, and two emerges from one. The division of two into one to act as the substance all permeates through; this is detailed in the section on numbers.

### 4. The Five Elements are not yet the "Five Materials," so they can be Symbolized
Kong Yingda's commentary on the classic mostly maintains the views of earlier scholars. Therefore, although he points to seven, eight, nine, and six as the four, and believes that the division of the four acts as the substance <note>referring to the core structure of the divination process</note>—all of which permeates through, detailed in the section on numbers—his so-called "four" still points to water, fire, wood, and metal, so it also does not depart from the four elements.
